hypotheses.title: MagicLpAggregator._getReserves missing return statement
hypotheses.description: The internal `_getReserves()` function declares return values `(uint256, uint256)` but never returns them; the body only calls `pair.getReserves()` and discards the result. Solidity will return the default values (0, 0) for the named-but-unassigned returns. As a result, `latestAnswer()` computes `minAnswer * (0 + 0) / totalSupply()` = 0, so the aggregator always reports a price of 0.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any consumer of this aggregator (e.g. a Cauldron using it as its oracle) will read a price of 0. An attacker can then borrow the maximum amount of MIM against any collateral because the solvency check `collateralValue >= borrowValue * exchangeRate` becomes trivially satisfied when exchangeRate is 0 (or the collateral is valued at 0, depending on direction). Alternatively, liquidations can be triggered on healthy positions because the price is 0.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of funds from any Cauldron/lending market that uses this aggregator as its price source; all positions become instantly liquidatable or infinitely borrowable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `return pair.getReserves();` inside `_getReserves()`.

hypotheses.title: MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer uses min() of base/quote oracle answers
hypotheses.description: The aggregator takes `minAnswer = min(baseAnswerNormalized, quoteAnswerNormalized)` and multiplies it by the sum of reserves divided by total supply. This is not a valid LP token price formula. The correct LP price is `(baseReserve * basePrice + quoteReserve * quotePrice) / totalSupply`. Using the minimum of the two oracle answers systematically undervalues the LP token whenever the two underlying assets have different prices, and it also ignores the actual reserve composition.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker who knows the LP token is undervalued can borrow against it at a favorable rate, or a liquidator can seize collateral from a healthy borrower because the reported collateral value is artificially low. Conversely, if the min oracle is manipulated upward, the LP is overvalued and the protocol can be drained.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic mispricing of LP collateral leading to under-collateralized loans and wrongful liquidations; loss of funds for borrowers and lenders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the LP price as `(baseReserve * basePrice + quoteReserve * quotePrice) / totalSupply` using both oracle answers, not the minimum.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4.updateExchangeRate accepts zero rate from oracle
hypotheses.description: `updateExchangeRate()` sets `exchangeRate = rate` whenever the oracle returns `updated == true`, with no check that `rate > 0`. If the oracle returns a zero rate (e.g. due to a misconfigured aggregator like MagicLpAggregator, or a transient oracle failure that still reports `updated`), the cauldron's exchange rate becomes 0. In `_isSolvent`, the borrow side is multiplied by `_exchangeRate`, so a zero rate makes every position solvent regardless of debt, and in `liquidate` the collateral calculation also collapses.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker waits for (or induces) the oracle to return a zero rate with `updated == true`, then calls `borrow()` to take out the maximum MIM against minimal collateral, or calls `removeCollateral()` to drain collateral while remaining "solvent". The zero rate persists until the next successful oracle update.
hypotheses.impact: Complete draining of MIM from the cauldron and loss of all collateral; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `updateExchangeRate()`, require `rate > 0` before assigning to `exchangeRate`, or revert if the oracle returns zero.

hypotheses.title: LockingMultiRewards reward accounting uses boosted balance for share math
hypotheses.description: `_updateRewardsForUser` and `_updateRewardsForUsers` compute each user's reward share using `balanceOf(user)`, which includes the `lockingBoostMultiplerInBips` multiplier on locked balances, while `totalSupply()` also includes the same boost. However, `_getRewards` and `earned` use the same boosted balance, so a user who locks tokens receives rewards proportional to the boosted amount. The boost multiplier is applied to both numerator and denominator, but the boost is not backed by additional staking tokens, so the reward pool is over-distributed relative to actual staked tokens whenever locked balances exist. Since `notifyRewardAmount` funds a fixed `amount` per period, boosted users drain rewards faster than the linear schedule, leaving later claimers with insufficient funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a large amount with `lock_=true` to get the 3x boost. 2) Attacker waits for rewards to accrue. 3) Attacker calls `getRewards()` to claim boosted rewards. 4) Because `totalSupply()` includes the boost, the attacker's share of the fixed reward pool is inflated relative to actual tokens deposited, and the contract's reward token balance is depleted faster than the intended schedule, causing later honest stakers to receive less or fail to claim.
hypotheses.impact: Reward pool drained faster than intended; honest stakers receive reduced or zero rewards; contract may become insolvent for reward payouts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Distribute rewards based on actual staked token amounts (unboosted) or ensure the boost is funded by an external source; do not use boosted balances in reward-per-token math.

hypotheses.title: MagicLpAggregator.latestRoundData returns zero timestamps and roundId
hypotheses.description: `latestRoundData()` returns `(0, latestAnswer(), 0, 0, 0)`. Consumers that check `updatedAt` for staleness (a standard Chainlink pattern) will see `updatedAt == 0` and either revert or treat the price as infinitely stale. Consumers that check `answeredInRound >= roundId` will also fail. This breaks integration with any Cauldron or external protocol that performs standard staleness validation.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but any protocol integrating this aggregator with staleness checks will either revert (DoS) or, if it ignores the check, accept a price that may be stale. An attacker can exploit the DoS to prevent liquidations of their own unhealthy position, or to block other users from borrowing/withdrawing.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on liquidations and borrowing; potential accumulation of bad debt if liquidations are blocked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Return `block.timestamp` for `updatedAt` and a non-zero `roundId`/`answeredInRound`, or document that consumers must not perform staleness checks.

hypotheses.title: Cauldron liquidate() transfers collateral to swapper before pulling MIM
hypotheses.description: In `liquidate`, the cauldron transfers the liquidated collateral share to `to` (the attacker-chosen address / swapper) via `bentoBox.transfer`, then calls `swapper.swap(...)`, and only afterwards pulls the MIM `allBorrowShare` from `msg.sender`. Because the `swapper` and `to` are caller-controlled, the attacker gets custody of the collateral before being required to fund the repayment. The state updates (`userCollateralShare`, `userBorrowPart`, `totalBorrow`, `totalCollateralShare`) are done, but the actual MIM inflow is deferred, so the entire sequence is "flash-liquidation": collateral out first, repayment last.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious `ISwapperV2` and calls `cauldron.liquidate([victim],[maxPart], attacker, maliciousSwapper, data)`. 2) Cauldron sub's the victim's debt/collateral from accounting, then `bentoBox.transfer(collateral, cauldron, attacker, allCollateralShare)` moves the collateral to the attacker. 3) `maliciousSwapper.swap` is invoked with `msg.sender = attacker`; inside, attacker uses the received collateral (e.g. as a BentoBox share he can withdraw/borrow against, or via sich) while the cauldron still expects `allBorrowShare` of MIM from `msg.sender`. 4) Attacker sources MIM via flash loan, repays inside `swap` or afterwards, keeping the arbitrage / liquidation bonus. 5) Since liquidations in insolvent cauldrons leave residual bad debt, the attacker can pick and choose which positions to liquidate, only stepping in when the bonus exceeds repayment.
hypotheses.impact: Liquidators can extract the liquidation incentive at no capital cost via flash loans; combined with the sSpell distribution adding `distributionAmount` to `feesEarned` regardless of who ultimately pays, can accelerate cauldron insolvency and drain MIM/fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender` to have already transferred `allBorrowShare` MIM to the cauldron (or use a BentoBox-transfer-and-receive pattern where the cauldron pulls MIM before releasing collateral), or have the swapper act only as an intermediary that atomically supplies the MIM before the collateral leaves the cauldron.

hypotheses.title: MagicLP.sellShares callbacks before reserve sync enables siphon
hypotheses.description: `sellShares` computes `baseAmount`/`quoteAmount` from the live token balances and `totalSupply`, then burns the user's shares and transfers base+quote to `to`, then calls `ICallee(to).SellShareCall(...)`, and only after the callback calls `_sync()` to update `_BASE_RESERVE_`/`_QUOTE_RESERVE_`/TWAP. During the callback, `getReserves()` and `getMidPrice()`/`getPMMState()` still return the pre-sell (inflated) reserves even though the pool's balances already dropped. The callback also runs after `_BASE_TARGET_`/`_QUOTE_TARGET_` were reduced but before reserve refresh, so views can be internally inconsistent. A reentrant call inside `SellShareCall` (e.g. `flashLoan` or `buyShares`) will see stale state and can price off the pre-sale reserve.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a pool/contract that owns LP shares and calls `sellShares` with a malicious `to` whose `SellShareCall` re-enters the same pool via `flashLoan` or `buyShares`. 2) Inside the callback, `getReserves()` returns old (higher) reserve values; `querySellBase`/`querySellQuote` and any integrator reading `getMidPrice` (e.g. `MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer()`) also use the stale reserves since `_sync()` has not run. 3) The attacker uses the mispriced quote to buy shares cheaply (or borrow base/quote via `flashLoan` at unfavorable-for-pool terms). 4) `_sync()` then updates reserves, locking in the attacker's favorable price.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrage siphons value from LPs; oracles reading `getReserves`/`getMidPrice` misprice, potentially enabling collateral valuation overflow in `CauldronV4` / `MagicLpAggregator` consumers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_sync()` (and `_twapUpdate`) before the external `SellShareCall` callback, or wrap the pool in a reentrancy guard that blocks `buyShares`/`sellShares`/`flashLoan`/`sync` during the callback.

hypotheses.title: MasterContractManager nonce increments even on failed signature recovery
hypotheses.description: In `setMasterContractApproval`, the nonce is incremented inline inside the `abi.encode` call: `nonces[user]++`. Because Solidity evaluates this before `ecrecover`, a failed signature check still consumes the nonce. An attacker who observes a pending signed approval (e.g., in the mempool) can front-run it with the same signature but a deliberately invalid `v`/`r`/`s` combination (or by replaying the exact signature in a way that reverts), causing the nonce to increment and invalidating the legitimate user's signature. The user's approval transaction then reverts with "Invalid Signature".
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User signs an EIP-712 approval with nonce N and submits it. 2) Attacker sees the tx in mempool, extracts `(v, r, s)`, and submits a tx calling `setMasterContractApproval` with the same arguments but a corrupted signature (e.g., `v=0`). 3) The call reverts after `nonces[user]++` has already executed, consuming nonce N. 4) User's original tx now fails because the digest uses nonce N+1 but the signature was for N.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing/DoS of user approvals; user must re-sign with a new nonce.
hypotheses.recommendation: Read `nonces[user]` into a local variable, perform signature verification, and only increment the nonce after successful verification.

hypotheses.title: LockingMultiRewards.notifyRewardAmount uses wrong remaining time for rewardRate
hypotheses.description: When `block.timestamp < reward.periodFinish`, the code adds `_remainingRewardTime * reward.rewardRate` to `amount` where `_remainingRewardTime = nextEpoch() - block.timestamp`. But the leftover from the current period should be `(periodFinish - block.timestamp) * rewardRate`. Since `periodFinish` is set to a previous `nextEpoch()` and `nextEpoch()` advances each epoch, `_remainingRewardTime` can be much larger than the actual leftover time, inflating the carried-over amount and thus the new `rewardRate`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator (or anyone able to call notifyRewardAmount via operator role) can call it at the start of a new epoch while the previous period is still active. The inflated `amount` produces an inflated `rewardRate`, so stakers earn more than the tokens actually deposited, draining the contract's reward token balance (which may include staking token or other rewards).
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of rewards; contract becomes insolvent for reward payouts; stakers who claim later cannot be paid.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `reward.periodFinish - block.timestamp` for the leftover calculation, not `_remainingRewardTime`.

hypotheses.title: MagicLP buyShares first-depositor share calculation can be manipulated
hypotheses.description: In `buyShares`, when `totalSupply() == 0`, shares are computed as `quoteBalance < mulFloor(baseBalance, _I_) ? divFloor(quoteBalance, _I_) : baseBalance`. The function then mints 1001 shares to `address(0)` and subtracts 1001 from the user's shares. An attacker can front-run the first legitimate depositor by directly transferring tokens to the pool (donation) before calling `buyShares`, inflating `baseBalance`/`quoteBalance` and thus the computed `shares`. Because the 1001 dead shares are fixed, the attacker can manipulate the initial share price to their advantage, or cause the first depositor to receive fewer shares than expected.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `createPool`/`buyShares` transaction. 2) Attacker front-runs by transferring a large amount of base or quote tokens directly to the new pool address. 3) When the victim's `buyShares` executes, `baseBalance`/`quoteBalance` are inflated, changing the share calculation. 4) Attacker calls `buyShares` themselves or `sellShares` to extract value from the mispriced pool.
hypotheses.impact: First depositor receives fewer shares than fair; attacker can extract value via subsequent sellShares; pool initial pricing is skewed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a minimum liquidity lock or compute shares based on `baseInput`/`quoteInput` rather than raw balances; consider a virtual offset.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4.liquidate uses stale exchangeRate if oracle update fails
hypotheses.description: `liquidate()` calls `updateExchangeRate()` and uses the returned `_exchangeRate`. If the oracle returns `updated == false`, `updateExchangeRate()` returns the cached `exchangeRate` (which may be arbitrarily stale). The comment says "Oracle can fail but we still need to allow liquidations", but there is no bound on how stale the cached rate can be. An attacker can exploit a stale rate that is favorable to them (e.g. a rate that makes a healthy position appear insolvent, or an insolvent position appear healthy) to liquidate or avoid liquidation.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker monitors the oracle for a failure/staleness event. If the cached rate makes a target position appear insolvent, the attacker liquidates it and seizes collateral at a discount. If the cached rate makes their own position appear solvent, they avoid liquidation and can withdraw collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Wrongful liquidations of healthy positions (loss of collateral for victims) or avoidance of legitimate liquidations (bad debt accumulation).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a maximum staleness check (e.g. store `lastExchangeRateUpdate` and revert if `block.timestamp - lastUpdate > MAX_STALENESS`), or require `updated == true` for liquidations.

hypotheses.title: Cauldron cook() ACTION_CALL allows reentry into cook/borrow before solvency check
hypotheses.description: `cook()` executes a caller-supplied sequence of actions, with `status.needsSolvencyCheck` only checked at the very end of the loop. `ACTION_CALL` performs an arbitrary call to any non-blacklisted `callee` *within* the loop, so the attacker can call back into the same cauldron (or a second cauldron sharing the same BentoBox) before the final `_isSolvent` check runs. Because `addCollateral`, `_borrow`, `_removeCollateral` etc. are individual public/internal entrypoints and `cook()` is reentrant, an attacker can `borrow` (or `removeCollateral`) inside the callback and then have the outer call's final solvency check depend on modified state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker builds a `cook` sequence: `ACTION_ADD_COLLATERAL` (or borrow), `ACTION_CALL` to a malicious contract, then rely on the outer `status.needsSolvencyCheck`. 2) Inside the callback, re-enter `cook` with `ACTION_REMOVE_COLLATERAL` and `ACTION_BORROW` (or re-enter `liquidate` against themselves) using the same collateral. 3) Because each `cook` computes solvency only at the end of its own loop and the outer loop is still in flight, the attacker can temporarily have collateral counted twice or borrow against collateral that will be removed afterwards. 4) `_borrow` and `_removeCollateral` don't gate on solvency; only `solvent` modifier / final cook check do.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of borrowable MIM / extraction of collateral from an under-collateralized position, potentially draining the cauldron's MIM supply; BentoBox accounting can be left insolvent on that cauldron.
hypotheses.recommendation: Forbid reentrancy by adding a nonReentrant guard to `cook`, or evaluate solvency at the point each state-changing action occurs and disallow `cook`-within-`cook` via a reentrancy flag.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4.cook blacklistedCallees check bypass via nested calls
hypotheses.description: `cook` allows `ACTION_CALL` (30) to any callee that is not blacklisted. The blacklist only includes `bentoBox`, `this`, and the BentoBox owner. An untrusted attacker can therefore call arbitrary contracts, including a contract that re-enters BentoBox directly (using the Cauldron's BentoBox master-contract approval granted via `setMasterContractApproval` within the same `cook`), transferring the Cauldron's own shares or the Cauldron operator's tokens. The intent is to prevent the Cauldron from calling BentoBox functions, but the caller can simply call a proxy/target that itself calls BentoBox with `msg.sender = Cauldron` — so the blacklist on direct callee is bypassable by deploying a wrapper contract (the wrapper address is not blacklisted).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys `Wrapper` that forwards calls to BentoBox (e.g., `withdraw`/`transfer` on Cauldron's behalf). Attacker calls `cook` with `ACTION_BENTO_SETAPPROVAL` to approve the Cauldron as masterContract, then `ACTION_CALL` to Wrapper which calls `bentoBox.transfer(...)` using the Cauldron's approved authority to drain user balances on the Cauldron's behalf.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all collateral/MIM shares the Cauldron is approved to move, or manipulation of the Cauldron's BentoBox balances; direct loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `ACTION_CALL` targets to an allowlist rather than a blacklist, or prevent the Cauldron from granting itself BentoBox masterContract approval inside `cook`.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4 liquidate accepts attacker-chosen swapper without validation
hypotheses.description: `liquidate` transfers all liquidated collateral shares to `to` and, if `swapper != 0`, calls `swapper.swap(...)` on an arbitrary caller-supplied contract before pulling `allBorrowShare` from `msg.sender`. Since the swapper address is chosen by the untrusted caller with no whitelist, an attacker can pass a malicious swapper that re-enters BentoBox, re-enters the Cauldron, manipulates the exchange rate, or performs arbitrary state changes during the liquidation flow before MIM repayment is enforced.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `liquidate(users, parts, attacker, MaliciousSwapper, data)`. MaliciousSwapper.swap re-enters BentoBox/Cauldron (e.g., `updateExchangeRate` with a manipulated oracle, or `cook`) to alter accounting or positions, then returns; the final `bentoBox.transfer(magicInternetMoney, msg.sender, ...)` only checks share amount, not position solvency of the liquidated users being kept out of the attacker's reach.
hypotheses.impact: Manipulation of liquidation math, theft via reentrancy, or causing under-collateralized liquidations; potential insolvency of the Cauldron.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `swapper` to a whitelisted set approved by the owner, and/or use a reentrancy guard on `liquidate`.

hypotheses.title: MagicLP sellShares rounds target reserves up, favoring remaining LPs
hypotheses.description: In `sellShares`, `_BASE_TARGET_` and `_QUOTE_TARGET_` are reduced using `divCeil(totalShares)`, i.e., the target is reduced by a rounded-up amount. This means the remaining LPs' targets are reduced more than proportionally, which can cause the pool's internal target reserves to drift from actual reserves over many small withdrawals. An attacker can perform many tiny `sellShares` calls to systematically drain value from the pool by exploiting the rounding direction, since each call rounds the target reduction up while the actual token amounts are rounded down.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires a small number of LP shares. 2) Attacker repeatedly calls `sellShares` with the smallest possible `shareAmount`. 3) Each call rounds `_BASE_TARGET_`/`_QUOTE_TARGET_` reductions up while `baseAmount`/`quoteAmount` are rounded down. 4) Over many iterations, the attacker extracts more value than their fair share, leaving remaining LPs with a pool whose targets are misaligned with reserves.
hypotheses.impact: Value leakage from the pool to the attacker; remaining LPs' shares are worth less than expected.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round target reductions down (favor the pool) or use a consistent rounding direction for both target and amount calculations.

hypotheses.title: Router._validateDecimals underflows on quoteDecimals < baseDecimals
hypotheses.description: `_validateDecimals` computes `quoteDecimals - baseDecimals` in an unchecked subtraction context (Solidity 0.8 would normally revert, but the check is intended to catch the difference). If `quoteDecimals < baseDecimals`, the subtraction underflows and reverts with a panic rather than the intended `ErrDecimalsDifferenceTooLarge`. More importantly, the check only validates the difference in one direction, so a pool with baseDecimals=18 and quoteDecimals=6 is rejected, but the reverse (base=6, quote=18) is also rejected by underflow — meaning legitimate pools with large decimal differences in either direction cannot be created. This is a functional bug, but it also means the validation is asymmetric and can be bypassed by choosing token order.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker creating a pool with a large decimal difference can order the tokens so that the subtraction does not underflow but the difference still exceeds the intended maximum, or vice versa. This can lead to pools with extreme decimal mismatches that cause rounding errors in `previewCreatePool` and `_adjustAddLiquidity`, potentially allowing value extraction from LPs.
hypotheses.impact: Pools with extreme decimal mismatches can be created, leading to rounding errors and potential loss of funds for liquidity providers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `if (baseDecimals > quoteDecimals) { if (baseDecimals - quoteDecimals > MAX) revert; } else { if (quoteDecimals - baseDecimals > MAX) revert; }` to handle both directions safely.

hypotheses.title: DegenBox withdraw's ETH send allows reentrant drain of other users' shares
hypotheses.description: In the ETH branch of `withdraw`, state (`balanceOf`, `totals[token].base/elastic`) is written before the interaction — good — but the ETH send uses `to.call{value: amount}("")` with all gas, and `allowed(from)` only checks that `from == msg.sender` or `from == address(this)` or an approved masterContract. Because `from == address(this)` is permitted (skim semantics), a malicious recipient contract that receives the ETH inside the `to.call` can re-enter `withdraw(USE_ETHEREUM, address(this), attacker, ...)` and drain any ETH that the box holds beyond `totals[WETH].elastic`. Even without `from == address(this)`, the recipient can re-enter other flows (`flashLoan`, `deposit`, `transfer`) while the calling contract's own accounting is mid-update.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits WETH, then withdraws as ETH with `to` = attacker contract. 2) Inside the ETH receive hook, call back `degenBox.withdraw(USE_ETHEREUM, address(this), attacker, x, 0)` — the skim path — claiming any ETH that has arrived in the box from other users' concurrent deposits/withdrawals/fee flows. 3) Because `_tokenBalanceOf` is computed via `token.balanceOf(address(this)) + strategyData[token].balance` and the check `amount <= _tokenBalanceOf(token) - total.elastic` uses current state, the attacker can skim the difference at any moment the box's real balance exceeds `total.elastic` (e.g. just-received deposits). 4) Repeat inside the callback for each margin available.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of ETH/WETH held in DegenBox, including pending deposits and stranded balances; users' deposited funds can be drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send ETH via a pull pattern (credit recipient's internal balance) or wrap the ETH send with a nonReentrant guard covering all state-mutating external entrypoints; consider disallowing `from == address(this)` for `USE_ETHEREUM` when the receiver is not the box itself, or require `msg.sender == to`.

hypotheses.title: MagicLP uses tx.origin for fee rate lookup enabling fee bypass
hypotheses.description: `sellBase` and `sellQuote` pass `tx.origin` as the `trader` argument to `querySellBase`/`querySellQuote`, which forwards it to `_MT_FEE_RATE_MODEL_.getFeeRate(trader, ...)`. A fee-rate implementation that grants discounts to specific EOAs (e.g., whitelisted traders) can be bypassed by routing through an intermediary contract, since `tx.origin` is the original EOA but the actual caller is the intermediary. Conversely, an attacker can also impersonate a discounted EOA's `tx.origin` by having that EOA call a malicious contract that invokes the pool, causing the pool to apply the discount to the attacker's trade.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `MagicLP.sellBase(to)`. 2) `tx.origin` is the attacker's EOA, but the fee model may apply a discount intended for a different context. 3) Alternatively, a discounted EOA is tricked into calling an attacker contract that performs the swap, so the pool applies the discount to the attacker's trade. 4) Attacker pays reduced LP/maintainer fees.
hypotheses.impact: Fee revenue loss for LPs and maintainer; incorrect fee accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `msg.sender` instead of `tx.origin` for the trader parameter, or explicitly document that fee models must not rely on `tx.origin`.

hypotheses.title: LockingMultiRewards._getRewards misaligns reward items when tokens added
hypotheses.description: The function assumes `_rewardLock.items[i]` corresponds to `rewardTokens[i]`. When a new reward token is added by the owner, existing users' `items` arrays are shorter than `rewardTokens`, so the `i < rewardItemLength` branch matches items to the wrong tokens for indices beyond the original length. Additionally, when `expired` is true and a new token is pushed, the item is appended but the loop index `i` may not match the item's position in the array for subsequent iterations.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner adds a new reward token after users have locked rewards. A user calls `getRewards()`; the loop reads `_rewardLock.items[i]` for `i` beyond the original item count, matching the wrong token to the wrong item, and transfers the wrong reward token amount or locks the wrong amount.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive wrong reward tokens/amounts; accounting corruption; potential loss of funds for users or the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the token address inside `RewardLockItem` and match by token address rather than by index.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4.init is publicly callable on master contract clone-front-run
hypotheses.description: `init(bytes)` is a public function with only the guard `require(address(collateral) == address(0))`. Any untrusted caller can call it via the BentoBox `deploy` flow on a fresh clone, but more importantly, on the master contract itself a call is blocked only because `collateral` was never set — however, clones created through BentoBox `deploy` are init'd by BentoBox in `deploy`, so an attacker cannot directly front-run. The real exposure: because `init` has no `msg.sender == bentoBox` check, anyone can call `init` on a freshly-deployed clone that hasn't yet been initialized in the same transaction. In practice BentoBox does it atomically, but any clone deployed outside that path is attacker-initializable.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes/searches for an uninitialized CauldronV4 clone (e.g., created via alternative deployment paths, or the master contract's clone factory flow where deployment and init are split) and calls `init` with attacker-chosen collateral/oracle/rates, capturing all future deposits for that clone.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker takes full control of the clone's parameters (oracle, collateral, interest rate, liquidation multiplier, LTV), enabling theft of user deposits and complete insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(msg.sender == address(bentoBox))` (or the deployer) in `init`, and require `masterContract != this` guard so the logic-only init is rejected.

hypotheses.title: DegenBox registerProtocol allows arbitrary msg.sender self-registration as master contract
hypotheses.description: `registerProtocol()` is `public` with no access control and sets `masterContractOf[msg.sender] = msg.sender`. This means any untrusted attacker can register as their own master contract. Combined with the `allowed(from)` modifier in DegenBox — which permits transfer/withdraw/deposit when `masterContractOf[msg.sender] != 0` AND `masterContractApproved[masterContract][from]` — the attacker only needs the victim to have previously approved the attacker's "master contract" (which the attacker can also self-approve via `setMasterContractApproval` fallback if the attacker's address is whitelisted, or via signed approval if the victim signed). More critically, the fallback path in `setMasterContractApproval` only requires `whitelistedMasterContracts[masterContract]`; but the signed path requires the victim's signature. The registration itself does not grant authorization without approval, but it removes the primary defense that only vetted contracts can be master contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `registerProtocol()`, becoming their own master contract. If the attacker can trick a user into signing a `SetMasterContractApproval` message for the attacker's address, the attacker can then move the victim's BentoBox shares via `transfer`, `withdraw`, or `deposit` (as `from`).
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all of a victim's BentoBox shares/MIM/collateral if the victim signs a phishing approval or if the victim's address is ever used as `from` in a DegenBox call.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `registerProtocol` be called only via an approved factory/owner-gated allowlist, or gate usage in `allowed(from)` by checking the master contract is whitelisted.

hypotheses.title: LockingMultiRewards notifyRewardAmount can be gamed to dilute existing rewards
hypotheses.description: `notifyRewardAmount` computes `reward.rewardRate = amount / _remainingRewardTime` and sets `periodFinish = _nextEpoch`. When called mid-period, it adds `_remainingRewardTime * reward.rewardRate` to `amount`, effectively rolling over unclaimed rewards. However, the division truncates, and an operator (or anyone with operator role) can call this repeatedly with tiny amounts to reset `lastUpdateTime` and `periodFinish`, causing rounding losses that accumulate. More importantly, an attacker who is an operator can call `notifyRewardAmount` with a very small `amount` right before `_nextEpoch` to reset the period and dilute the reward rate for existing stakers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (operator) calls `notifyRewardAmount` with `amount = _remainingRewardTime` (minimum) repeatedly. 2) Each call resets `lastUpdateTime` and `periodFinish`, and the integer division `amount / _remainingRewardTime` truncates. 3) Existing stakers' accrued rewards are recalculated against a lower effective rate, diluting their share.
hypotheses.impact: Existing stakers receive fewer rewards than expected; reward accounting drifts from intended schedule.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a higher-precision accumulator or require a minimum notify interval; avoid resetting `lastUpdateTime` on every call.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4 liquidate distribution fee double-counts borrow amount
hypotheses.description: In `liquidate`, after computing `allBorrowAmount`, the code computes `distributionAmount = (allBorrowAmount * LIQUIDATION_MULTIPLIER / LIQUIDATION_MULTIPLIER_PRECISION - allBorrowAmount) * DISTRIBUTION_PART / DISTRIBUTION_PRECISION`, then adds it to `allBorrowAmount` and to `accrueInfo.feesEarned`. However, `allBorrowAmount` is then used to compute `allBorrowShare` via `bentoBox.toShare(magicInternetMoney, allBorrowAmount, true)`, meaning the liquidator must pay the distribution fee on top of the liquidation amount. The fee is added to `feesEarned` but the liquidator's payment includes it, so the fee is effectively charged to the liquidator and also recorded as protocol fees, potentially double-counting if the liquidator is also a fee recipient or if the fee is later withdrawn.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (liquidator) liquidates a user. 2) The distribution fee is added to `allBorrowAmount` and to `feesEarned`. 3) The liquidator pays `allBorrowShare` which includes the distribution fee. 4) If the liquidator is also the `feeTo` or can withdraw fees, they can recover the fee, effectively paying less than the full liquidation amount while the protocol records the fee as earned.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol fee accounting is inflated; liquidator may pay less than intended; MIM balance in the cauldron may drift from `feesEarned`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Separate the distribution fee from the liquidator's payment amount, or ensure `feesEarned` reflects only the net fee actually retained by the protocol.

hypotheses.title: LockingMultiRewards notifyRewardAmount uses pre-transfer reward balance
hypotheses.description: `notifyRewardAmount` calls `_updateRewards()` (global reward-per-token update), then `rewardToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)`, and then computes `reward.rewardRate` from the passed `amount` plus `_remainingRewardTime * reward.rewardRate` (if the prior period hasn't finished). Because `_updateRewards` only updates `rewardPerTokenStored` using the *old* `rewardRate`, both the transfer and the `_updateRewards` happen before the new rate is set. If the reward token is a hook-capable / malicious ERC-20 (or if an operator is untrusted), the token's `transferFrom` can reenter the staking contract (e.g. `stake`/`getRewards`) while `_rewardData[rewardToken].rewardPerTokenStored` is up-to-date but `reward.periodFinish`/`rewardRate` are stale. Users who call `stake`/`getRewards` in that window accrue rewards under the old rate for elapsed time that should already have been captured; then `lastUpdateTime`/`periodFinish` changes, double-counting or missing pending rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Malicious reward token's `transferFrom` calls back into `LockingMultiRewards.stake(...)` or `getRewards()` for the attacker. 2) Inside the callback, `_updateRewardsForUser` uses the *old* `periodFinish`/`rewardRate` (because `notifyRewardAmount` hasn't yet written the new ones) and credits the attacker using `lastTimeRewardApplicable` = old `periodFinish`. 3) After the callback returns, `notifyRewardAmount` sets the new `periodFinish = nextEpoch()` and `lastUpdateTime = block.timestamp`, but the elapsed-time window between old `periodFinish` and `block.timestamp` at the reentrant update was already partially captured for the attacker's action and will be captured again by the next global update.
hypotheses.impact: Reward dilution: some stakers receive less than earned, others (attacker) receive more; could drain rewards over time and leave `rewards[user][token]` inconsistent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `safeTransferFrom` and the `_updateRewards()` call after writing `reward.rewardRate`, `lastUpdateTime`, `periodFinish` — or use a reentrancy guard on `notifyRewardAmount` / `stake` / `getRewards`.

hypotheses.title: NotifyRewardAmount mixes remaining rewards into new period, gifting unearned rewards
hypotheses.description: When adding rewards before the current period finishes, `amount += _remainingRewardTime * reward.rewardRate` credits already-emitted-but-unclaimed rewards back into the new period's `rewardRate`, while `_updateRewardsGlobal` has already checkpointed `rewardPerTokenStored` on the old period. Rewards that are still pending for existing stakers under the old rate get double-counted, and the new period's `rewardRate = amount / _remainingRewardTime` is inflated. Since rewardsDuration is immutable and notify is operator-driven, the accounting inconsistency is baked into every top-up.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Stakers hold positions during the current period. 2) Before period end, any operator (or compromised operator path) calls notifyRewardAmount, which folds remaining rate*time into new amount. 3) rewardPerTokenStored reflects the entire old period while the new period now pays out the same time window again, diluting prior accrued rewards for users who claim after the notify. A user that times a claim just before notify captures old-rate rewards, and after notify the same time window is re-funded, so late claimers receive less than they earned and rate inflates.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution; rewards claimed at wrong times are over/under-paid; possible reward token over-spend/drain of reward pool relative to tokens transferred.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track already-accrued (unemitted) remainder separately and only add genuinely new funding to the new period; do not add `_remainingRewardTime * rewardRate` to `amount` while also preserving rewardPerTokenStored for the same interval.

hypotheses.title: WithdrawFees sends entire fee balance including MIM reserved as flashloan fees/collateral
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFees()` transfers `accrueInfo.feesEarned` MIM shares out of the cauldron without checking that the cauldron actually holds that free MIM. Borrow opening fees are stored in MIM elastic, but the cauldron's balance of MIM in BentoBox is exactly what remains after all loans are outstanding. If outstanding borrows (or active flash liquidations) leave less MIM than feesEarned in the box, calling withdrawFees drains shares that belong to active borrowers' repayment reserves, effectively socializing a loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Borrower opens position (fee accrues in feesEarned). 2) MIM balance in the cauldron shrinks due to other borrowers' drawdowns (borrow transfers out from address(this) in `_borrow`). 3) Anyone (the feeTo recipient or master contract owner path, but the transfer reverts or drains; note feeTo receives unconditionally) allows withdrawFees to be triggered; the function subtracts feesEarned MIM share from the cauldron even though loans are outstanding, transferring out MIM that is implicitly backing the borrowers' debt. Since BentoBox share accounting is global, this reduces MIM available for repay flows and forces later repayers to top-up the shortfall.
hypotheses.impact: Cauldron MIM shortfall; later borrower repayments or liquidations may revert or require more MIM than expected; insolvency gap between totalBorrow and MIM held.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap withdrawFees to the free MIM share actually held in the cauldron (BentoBox balance minus the MIM needed to satisfy totalBorrow obligations), or segregate fee accounting from the pool's MIM reserve.

hypotheses.title: DegenBox strategy setStrategy applies profit to all holders before strategy actually realized
hypotheses.description: When changing a strategy, `setStrategy` calls `strategy[token].exit(data.balance)` and immediately applies positive `balanceChange` to `totals[token].elastic` as profit (or subtracts on loss). `exit` is fully controlled by the outgoing strategy, and the profit/loss is applied to the global rebase *after* the exit interaction but with `data.balance` (the bookkeeping value) — not the actual returned amount. Any user who observces a profitable strategy can front-run its exit / setStrategy by depositing large size right before the profit is applied and withdrawing just after, capturing a proportional share of the injected profit as a bystander. Conversely, a loss can be escaped by withdrawing right before `setStrategy` when the loss is already known off-chain.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker watches mempool / on-chain state for a pending `setStrategy` that will call `exit` with positive balanceChange. 2) Before the tx lands, attacker deposits a large amount into the token pool (shares minted at old share value). 3) After the tx, shares are worth more due to `addElastic(add)`; attacker withdraws at the inflated share price. 4) Profit for attacker is proportionally taken from existing LPs; they can repeat for every strategy transition.
hypotheses.impact: Yield/strategy PnL is farmed by flash-timing around strategy transitions, diluting long-term LPs and letting insiders/observers extract strategy profits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track pending strategy PnL separately and only distribute on harvest; or snapshot share supply at the time the strategy's PnL is realized with a time-lock so deposits/withdrawals cannot straddle the event.

hypotheses.title: BlastOnboardingBoot.claim uses stale totalPoolShares after staking changes
hypotheses.description: `_claimable()` computes `shares = userLocked * totalPoolShares / totalLocked`. `totalPoolShares` is set once during `bootstrap()` and never updated. If the staking contract's total supply changes (e.g., via `setStaking` or if the pool's total supply changes), the ratio becomes stale. Also, `totalLocked` is read from `totals[MIM].locked + totals[USDB].locked` which is the onboarding contract's locked totals, not the staking contract's actual supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: After bootstrap, if the owner changes the staking contract via `setStaking`, `totalPoolShares` still refers to the old pool's shares. Users claiming will receive shares computed against the old pool's total, but `staking.stakeFor` will stake into the new staking contract, potentially minting incorrect amounts or reverting.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive wrong share amounts; potential loss of funds or inability to claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute or update `totalPoolShares` when the staking contract changes, or read the actual pool total supply at claim time.

hypotheses.title: BlastOnboarding Proxy _implementation returns mutable untrusted bootstrapper
hypotheses.description: `BlastOnboarding` inherits `Proxy` and overrides `_implementation()` to return `address(bootstrapper)`, an operator-set value. While `setBootstrapper` is `onlyOwner`, once the bootstrapper is set it becomes the delegatecall target for all fallback calls. The user-facing `deposit`/`lock`/`withdraw` are defined in `BlastOnboarding` itself (not routed through the proxy), but all other calls — including potentially sensitive functions expected to be on the bootstrap contract — delegate to the bootstrapper. If the bootstrapper is ever set to a malicious or compromised address (or if the bootstrapper's `claim`/`bootstrap` functions are re-used), user funds stored in this contract (all token balances) are exposed to whatever code the bootstrapper contains. More importantly, `receive()` is overridden to revert, but the Proxy fallback still delegates; there is no `_implementation` change guard requiring the bootstrapper to be audited. The concern is that the bootstrapper is the delegatecall target for the entire contract's fallback.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a non-owner path ever causes `bootstrapper` to be set (or if a bootstrapper value is set post-audit without re-audit), any external caller invoking an unrecognized function selector on BlastOnboarding triggers `fallback` -> `delegatecall` into the bootstrapper, which executes with this contract's storage and can transfer out `balances`-tracked tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Total loss of deposited user funds held in BlastOnboarding.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document and freeze the bootstrapper once set, and make the proxy upgrade path require a timelock plus verification; alternatively implement a whitelist of delegatecall selectors.

hypotheses.title: BlastOnboardingBoot.claim is unrestricted and uses router-created pool state
hypotheses.description: `claim(bool lock)` has no access control, which is intended (each user claims their own), but it relies entirely on `claimed[msg.sender]` and `_claimable`. The `_claimable` computation uses `totalPoolShares` set by `bootstrap()` and the user's locked balances. If `bootstrap` is front-run or `setStaking` is changed after users have begun deposit but before `bootstrap`, the newly set `staking` contract could be malicious (owner-set) and `stakeFor` calls transfer user LP shares to it. More relevant to untrusted actors: `claim` mints/provides staking shares proportional to `totalPoolShares / totalLocked`. Any untrusted user who can manipulate `balances[user][MIM].locked` or `balances[user][USDB].locked` (e.g., by depositing with `lock_ = true` after `ready` but before bootstrap — which is allowed by `deposit` while state is Opened, but bootstrap requires Closed, so not directly exploitable) can inflate their claim. Given `bootstrap` requires `State.Closed` and `deposit` requires `State.Opened`, the ordering prevents post-close inflation; however `setStaking` and `bootstrap` race conditions remain.
hypotheses.attackPath: If owner calls `bootstrap` with a staking contract that is malicious (owner collusion or mistake), all claiming users' LP shares are handed to it. Untrusted-user-only path is limited.
hypotheses.impact: Potential loss of pooled LP shares to an unintended staking contract; incorrect accounting if bootstrap ordering is subverted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `bootstrap` deploy the staking contract and immediately transfer ownership in the same tx (already done), and freeze `staking` strictly before `ready`; add a timelock or event-emitted 2-step for setStaking.

hypotheses.title: DegenBox deposit with share=0 and small amount can be griefed via MINIMUM_SHARE_BALANCE
hypotheses.description: In `deposit`, when `share == 0`, the function computes `share = total.toBase(amount, false)` and then checks `if (total.base.add(share.to128()) < MINIMUM_SHARE_BALANCE) return (0, 0);`. This means a deposit that would result in a total share balance below 1000 is silently ignored (no tokens taken, no shares minted). An attacker can exploit this by making a tiny deposit to a fresh token pool to keep `total.base` below `MINIMUM_SHARE_BALANCE`, preventing legitimate small deposits from being processed. More importantly, if a user deposits an amount that rounds down to 0 shares, they receive nothing but the function returns (0,0) without reverting, which can confuse integrators.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a tiny amount of a new token to a fresh DegenBox token pool, keeping `total.base` just below 1000. 2) Legitimate users attempting small deposits get `(0,0)` returned and their tokens are not taken, but their transaction succeeds silently. 3) Integrators relying on the return value may mis-account.
hypotheses.impact: Small deposits are silently ignored; integrators may mis-handle zero-share deposits; potential for griefing on new token pools.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on zero-share deposits or emit an event; consider a minimum deposit amount check.

hypotheses.title: Router.addLiquidityETH refund sent before token pull enables ETH skim
hypotheses.description: `addLiquidityETH` computes the adjusted amounts, deposits the WETH-adjusted amount into WETH and transfers it to the LP, then refunds leftover ETH to the attacker-supplied `refundTo` via `safeTransferETH`, and only afterwards pulls `tokenAdjustedAmount` of `token` from `msg.sender` via `safeTransferFrom`. If `token` is a hook-capable ERC-20, its `transferFrom` executes after the refund; more importantly, if `refundTo` is a contract, the ETH refund is an external call to an attacker-controlled address while the subsequent `token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, lp, ...)` still needs to succeed. The attacker can make the refund trigger arbitrary code (reentrancy into Router/LP) before the token side of the LP deposit is funded, and can also make the refund amount itself `msg.value - wethAdjustedAmount` which is attacker-tunable via the ratio between `msg.value` and `tokenInAmount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addLiquidityETH{value: X}(lp, to, refundTo=malicious, tokenInAmount=..., ...)`. 2) The pair-adjustment logic may choose to `wethAdjustedAmount < msg.value`, sending the remainder to the malicious contract. 3) Inside the malicious `receive()`/fallback, reenter `Router` or `MagicLP` to interact with the pool state that is already updated (WETH deposited), under conditions where the matched `token` pull has not yet occurred — e.g. call `sellBase`/`sellQuote` at mispriced state before the pool receives the intended token input. 4) The subsequent `token.safeTransferFrom` may revert or succeed at a ratio the attacker has engineered.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker obtains a favorable swap/LP position, or causes a failed-but-partially-executed LP flow (WETH in the pool, no token side) leaving LP reserves skewed and other LPs' shares mispriced.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pull the `token` side from `msg.sender` *before* refunding ETH, and/or don't send ETH refunds to arbitrary addresses inside the LP-add flow (require `refundTo == msg.sender`, or accumulate refunds and send through a guarded path).

hypotheses.title: Router.removeLiquidity lacks ensureDeadline modifier
hypotheses.description: `removeLiquidity` does not have the `ensureDeadline(deadline)` modifier, unlike `addLiquidity`, `addLiquidityUnsafe`, `addLiquidityETH`, `swapTokensForTokens`, etc. The `deadline` parameter is passed to `IMagicLP(lp).sellShares(...)`, which does check `deadline < block.timestamp` and reverts with `ErrExpired`. However, the Router itself does not enforce the deadline before transferring LP shares from `msg.sender` to itself. If `sellShares` reverts, the entire transaction reverts, so the shares are not lost. But the missing modifier means the Router's own deadline check is absent; the only protection is the pool's check. If a pool implementation does not enforce the deadline (e.g., a malicious or upgraded pool), the Router would execute without deadline protection.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A user calls `removeLiquidity` with a deadline that has already passed. 2) The Router transfers LP shares from the user to itself. 3) The Router calls `sellShares` on the pool. 4) If the pool does not enforce the deadline (e.g., a non-standard or malicious pool), the removal executes at an unfavorable time, potentially after a price manipulation. 5) The user receives less than expected.
hypotheses.impact: Users may have their liquidity removed at an unfavorable time if the pool does not enforce the deadline; loss of funds due to price manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the `ensureDeadline(deadline)` modifier to `removeLiquidity` and `removeLiquidityETH` for consistency and defense-in-depth.

hypotheses.title: CauldronV4 cook ACTION_BENTO_SETAPPROVAL allows arbitrary signature replay
hypotheses.description: The `cook` function's `ACTION_BENTO_SETAPPROVAL` action decodes `(user, _masterContract, approved, v, r, s)` and calls `bentoBox.setMasterContractApproval(user, _masterContract, approved, v, r, s)`. The `user` is an arbitrary address supplied by the caller, not necessarily `msg.sender`. While `setMasterContractApproval` verifies the signature against `user` and uses a nonce, the `cook` function allows any caller to submit a valid signature on behalf of `user`. If a user has signed an approval for a different `masterContract` or a different `approved` value, an attacker cannot directly reuse it because the digest includes those fields. However, the nonce is consumed by the `setMasterContractApproval` call, and the `cook` function does not restrict who can call it. This is not a direct replay vulnerability because the signature is bound to the specific parameters and nonce. The real issue is that `cook` can be used to consume a user's nonce without their consent if the attacker obtains a valid signature, but that requires the signature. No direct exploit without a signature.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid signature from a user for `setMasterContractApproval` (e.g., from a previous transaction or a phishing attempt). 2) Attacker calls `cook` with `ACTION_BENTO_SETAPPROVAL` and the user's signature. 3) The nonce is consumed, and the approval is set. 4) If the signature was for a different `masterContract` or `approved` value, the call reverts. 5) If the signature matches, the approval is set as intended. This is not a vulnerability per se, but the `cook` function allows anyone to submit the approval, which could be used for griefing if the user intended to submit it themselves.
hypotheses.impact: Potential griefing if an attacker consumes a user's nonce by front-running their approval transaction with the same signature via `cook`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Consider restricting `ACTION_BENTO_SETAPPROVAL` to `msg.sender == user` or requiring that the caller is the user, to prevent front-running and nonce consumption by third parties.

hypotheses.title: Borrow opening fee is added to elastic but distributed as cash only on liquidation path
hypotheses.description: `_borrow` increases `totalBorrow.elastic` by `amount + feeAmount` and adds `feeAmount` to `accrueInfo.feesEarned`. The MIM is only ever sent out as `amount`; the fee never enters BentoBox as cash. When a borrower is later liquidated, `allBorrowAmount` includes the opening fee (since it maps to elastic) and only that amount plus a distribution fee is subtracted from `totalBorrow.elastic`. `feesEarned` still holds the opening fee PLUS the liquidation distribution, so on withdrawFees the cauldron must send more MIM than actually exists (the opening fee was never deposited). The user's repay path does transfer fee via elastic rebase, but the fee was accrued against MIM shares they only later provide — meanwhile feesEarned is treated as immediately claimable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) opens a large position with high BORROW_OPENING_FEE. feesEarned jumps by feeAmount. 2) feeTo calls withdrawFees before enough repays have supplied the MIM backing that fee; shares are paid out from the cauldron's remaining MIM (which belongs to other borrowers' collateralized MIM reserve). 3) Shortfall materializes as an accounting gap between accrual and actual MIM inflow.
hypotheses.impact: Fees are claimable before the underlying MIM exists, draining MIM that is required to back the loan book. This is a solvency leak that can be triggered whenever opening fees are non-zero.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only count the opening fee in `feesEarned` as it is actually repaid, or ensure the cauldron deposits equivalent MIM as the opening fee is booked.

hypotheses.title: getLiquidationCollateralAndBorrowAmount never returns adjustedBorrowPart despite docstring
hypotheses.description: The function documents clamping borrowPart to available collateral via `maxBorrowPart` and returning `adjustedBorrowPart`, but at the end it simply does `adjustedBorrowPart = borrowPart` where `borrowPart` is the local variable that was possibly capped — however the cap computation `maxBorrowPart` uses `totalBorrow.toBase(...)` on the whole max, so any off-chain consumer (and integrations that use this helper for liquidations) assumes a properly bounded part. Worse, the same function is used by callers expecting `requiredMim` to exactly cover the position; the MIM amount is recomputed via extra "distribution part" adjustment but the caller in `liquidate` reads fees from `LIQUIDATION_MULTIPLIER` directly, so any integration using this helper mis-computes liquidation requirements. Because liquidate() in CauldronV4 does not cap by underlying collateral at all, a liquidator can attempt to seize more collateral share than the user owns and `userCollateralShare[user].sub(collateralShare)` will revert after the debt sub has already been recorded in some flows, or the sSpell distribution is charged against MIM the liquidator never provides.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker spots a position where collateralShare < borrowAmount * LIQ_MULT * rate. 2) Calls liquidate with maxBorrowParts exceeding what collateral supports. 3) The loop subtracts userBorrowPart and userCollateralShare; if the collateral share sub underflows the whole tx reverts, but if it just equals it, the cauldron still records allBorrowAmount including the sSpell distribution — the liquidator didn't pay for that distribution. Net: liquidator under-pays by ~10% of the liquidation bonus while walking away with the collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Under-payment of borrowed MIM by liquidator; bad debt and MIM shortfall are pushed onto the cauldron.
hypotheses.recommendation: In CauldronV4.liquidate clamp `collateralShare` to `userCollateralShare[user]` and recompute borrowAmount/borrowPart consistently, or use `getLiquidationCollateralAndBorrowAmount` correctly and honor the returned adjusted part.
